paper_title: Embedding Physics Priors in Robot Learning: A Survey

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The rapid progress of artificial intelligence is reshaping robotics and accelerating the adoption of learning-based approaches. While purely data-driven methods have achieved remarkable success in computer vision and natural language processing, robotics remains constrained by limited data, complex real-world interactions, and the need for reliable operation. These challenges have motivated the exploration of physics-embedded robot learning, which embeds physics priors into learning algorithms. By encoding the underlying physical laws and constraints, physics priors can complement limited data with robotics-specific inductive biases, potentially improving generalization, interpretability, and sample efficiency. However, the literature on physics-embedded robot learning remains fragmented across terminology, methodologies, and application domains, making it difficult to assess this growing body of work. This survey reviews physics-embedded robot learning across a broad range of physics priors, robotics applications, and machine learning models, from single-layer perceptrons to generative foundation models. We adopt a unified taxonomy that classifies existing approaches according to their physics embedding: physics-guided inputs, data, and representations; physics-encoded model architectures; and physics-informed training loss functions. Building on this taxonomy, we review methods for robot dynamics learning, trajectory planning, prediction, control, and estimation, together with the corresponding open-source software ecosystem. We identify key open challenges, and outline promising future research directions. Overall, we argue that physics priors provide a particularly relevant robotics-specific inductive bias, complementing rather than replacing data-driven learning, and paving the way toward more generalizable, data-efficient, and trustworthy robotic systems.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The remarkable success of Machine Learning (ML), from deep learning to foundation models, has shown that scaling data and computation can unlock unprecedented performance across diverse domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and strategic games (He et al. 2016; Brown et al. 2020; Schrittwieser et al. In 2020; Vinyals et al. 2019; Jumper et al. 2021). robotics, however, collecting training data is expensive due to the cost of real-world experiments, specialized hardware, human supervision, and safety constraints. Furthermore, robots are often high-dimensional systems: for example, dexterous robot hand may have more than 20 Degrees of Freedom (DoF), resulting in complex dynamics with nonlinearities, underactuation, and hybrid contact modes. Combined with the scarcity of large-scale open datasets and the need for real-time operation in safetycritical environments, these challenges make it difficult to rely solely on robot data and computation while ensuring safe generalization to unseen scenarios (Billard et al. 2025; Goldberg 2025). Because robots are embodied agents governed by physical laws, physics provides natural domain-specific inductive bias. We first define the scope of the reviewed literature (Sec. 1.1), compare our work with existing surveys (Sec. 1.2), summarize our contributions (Sec. 1.3), and provide historical overview of physics-embedded robot learning (Sec. 1.4). Sec. 2 then introduces the three main physics-embedding routes for robot learning that underpin the taxonomy of our survey. sections.content: Our survey focuses on ML approaches that embed physics priors and are applied to robotics. Prepared using sagej.cls Types of Physics Priors: We consider broad range of physics priors, grouped into five non-mutually exclusive families. (i) Governing equations: Newton-Euler, EulerLagrange, Hamiltonian, and port-Hamiltonian formulations, together with the Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) and Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) describing rigidbody and continuum systems. (ii) Conservation laws, symmetries, and invariances: conservation of energy, momentum, and power, together with symmetry, invariance, and equivariance principles (e.g., SE(3), SO(3), and morphological symmetries). (iii) Geometric and kinematic structure: manifolds and Lie groups, kinematic trees, subsystem decompositions, connectivity and modularity of multibody systems, and holonomic and nonholonomic constraints. (iv) Constitutive and interaction models: friction, contact and impact laws, stiffness, damping, material behavior, and actuator and drivetrain dynamics. (v) Physical consistency and admissibility: positive definiteness of inertia matrices, positive semi-definiteness of damping matrices, physically meaningful parameter bounds and sign constraints, passivity, dissipativity, stability properties, actuator limits, and boundary conditions. Generic mathematical representations alone are not considered physics priors unless they explicitly encode physical knowledge. sections.title: 1.3 Contributions
sections.content: To the best of our knowledge, none of the previously discussed surveys provides structured review of the broad spectrum of approaches embedding physics priors into robot learning methods. Our survey aims to fill this gap with the following contributions: structured review on embedding physics priors into robot learning methods and applications. We cover wide range of ML models, from singlelayer perceptrons to generative models, and broad spectrum of physics priors, from NewtonEuler and Lagrangian dynamics to conservation laws, symmetries, and invariances. classification of the existing literature into three categories, based on where physics priors are embedded: inputs, data, and representations (physicsguided), internal architectures (physics-encoded), and loss functions (physics-informed). categorization of the corresponding applications into robot dynamics learning, trajectory planning and prediction, control, and estimation, and an overview of the open-source software tools to support physicsembedded robot learning. An identification of the main challenges and open research questions. Based on our analysis, we propose future research directions to advance the field.

sections.title:
1.4 Historical Perspective: From Analytical
Models to Physics-Embedded Learning
sections.content: Analytical Models: For decades, robotics has relied primarily on analytical models derived from kinematics, rigid-body dynamics, and optimal control to describe and control physical systems (Siciliano and Khatib 2016). These models encode strong physics priors through kinematic and dynamic equations, conservation laws, and geometric constraints, providing interpretable representations and, in some cases, analytical guarantees for planning and control. However, their accuracy is limited by simplifying assumptions, unmodeled dynamics, and the complexity of real-world environments. et Data-Driven Robot Learning: Learning-based methods later emerged as complementary paradigm, using data to model phenomena that are difficult to capture analytically. Early applications employed NNs for including Cererobot control and dynamics modeling, bellar Model Arithmetic Computer (CMAC)-based controllers for manipulation and bipedal locomotion (Albus 1975; Miller and Kun 1997), al. 1987; Miller and Radial Basis Function Networks (RBFNs) for adaptive robot control (Broomhead and Lowe 1988; Sanner and Slotine 1995). Learning from demonstration further reduced the need for manually designed task models, while ALVINN (Pomerleau 1988) was an early example of end-to-end autonomous driving from sensor observations. The scalability of deep learning later marked major advance in robot learning. Following the success of deep CNNs (Krizhevsky et al. 2012), robotics adopted end-to-end visuomotor policies (Levine et al. 2016) and RL for complex manipulation (OpenAI et al. 2019). More recently, transformers, diffusion models, and foundation models have further expanded the capabilities and generality of robot learning (Vaswani et al. 2017; Chi et al. 2023), paving the way for VLAs , VWMs, and other multimodal approaches. Incorporating Domain Priors: The evolution of ML tailored inductive has repeatedly shown that scalable, biases embedded in ML architectures can improve learning efficiency without sacrificing expressive power. For example, CNNs encode translation invariance for image recognition, while LSTM recurrent architectures have specialized gating mechanisms to encode sequential dependencies. Since robots are embodied systems governed by physical laws, physics provides natural robotics-specific inductive bias. This has motivated methods that embed physics priors directly into ML algorithms. Early examples include NguyenTuong and Peters (2010), who incorporated rigid-body model as the mean function and kernel of Gaussian process for manipulator inverse dynamics learning, while Cheng et al. (2016) encoded the Lagrangian structure of the dynamics in reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Shortly thereafter, Dıaz Ledezma and Haddadin (2017, 2018) constructed network topologies from NewtonEuler operators, anticipating the physics-encoded architectures later formalized by DeLaN (Lutter et al. 2019b). These early ideas have since evolved into the physics-guided, physicsencoded, and physics-informed paradigms reviewed in this survey. Prepared using sagej.cls Figure 3. sections.title:
2 Physics-Guided, Physics-Encoded, and
Physics-Informed Robot Learning:
Overview and Organization
sections.content: Taxonomy: As anticipated in the introduction, we adapt the taxonomy of Faroughi et al. (2024) to classify physicsembedded robot learning into three categories, illustrated in Fig. 1. In our survey, Physics-guided learning exploits physics priors to transform, enrich, curate, select, or correct the inputs, data, or representations of learning models, either before training or as preor post-processing guidance at inference. Physics-encoded learning embeds physics directly into model architectures, via tailored structures, layers, and topologies, governing equations and structure-preserving integrators, geometric and kinematic structure, energy and conservation principles, symmetries and invariances, architectural constraints, or the composition of learnable components with analytical physics-based models. Finally, Physics-informed learning incorporates physics into the training objective, typically through regularization terms or residual losses derived from governing physical equations. Together, these three categories define physics-embedded learning, whose goal is to complement data with the available physics priors. Depending on the application, our taxonomy may be applied to the entire robot learning pipeline, an individual learning model, or specific submodule within larger architecture. Lifecycle of Physics Priors: Physics priors can be incorporated at different stages of the learning lifecycle, as illustrated in Fig. 3. We split the lifecycle into three stages: (i) data curation, (ii) model training, and (iii) inference. Physics-guided components transform, curate, or enrich input features and data through physically meaningful representations. They may be applied during data curation, or implemented as pre-processing modules that remain part of the training and inference pipelines. In the latter case, any learnable quantities of the pre-processing modules are pretrained or frozen when training the main model  (Fig. 1)  . Physics-encoded components embed physical knowledge directly into the model architecture, and therefore remain active during both training and inference. Finally, physics-informed residual loss terms are evaluated only during training. Their influence persists at inference only through the learned model parameters, but they do not affect the model architecture or input features  (Fig. 3)  . Classification Flow: To classify existing methods, we adopt the decision flow in Fig. 4. The three categories (physics-guided, physics-encoded, physics-informed) are not mutually exclusive, and method may belong to multiple categories. The same decision flow is implemented in our open-source repository to continuously classify newly published methods.

As the NNs that parameterize M(q) and V(q) take only as input, the dependence of the resulting forward and inverse dynamics models on velocities and accelerations is analytically determined by the Lagrangian formulation (3), rather than learned from data, improving generalization to unseen velocities and accelerations. By learning the Lagrangian terms, DeLaN improve energy conservation of unforced systems and long-term stability of learned dynamic models, while providing interpretable physical quantities such as M(q) and V(q). Training DeLaN for Forward and Inverse Dynamics: DeLaN do not only learn an energy model, but also provide forward and inverse dynamics models obtained via (2). As result, they can be trained using loss functions defined on any of these formulations, or on combination of them. This further enables their use within model-based frameworks based on (3). 3.1.2 Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs): Introduced
by Cranmer et al. (2020), LNNs learn the Lagrangian
L directly as an unstructured NN function of q and ˙q,
rather than imposing the energy decomposition in (1).
Unlike DeLaN, which assume the specific form (1) of the
Lagrangian and its kinetic energy (which works for certain
classes of systems like rigid bodies), LNNs can represent
more general Lagrangians, enabling dynamics learning
of charged particle systems and others. The generalized
accelerations ¨q are recovered from the learned Lagrangian
via (2), and the model is trained by minimizing the error
between predicted and measured accelerations. Cranmer

sections.content: Lu et al. (2022) proposed modular version of LNN by learning coordinate transformation map based on the known kinematic tree. Some authors used LNN and DeLaN for model-based RL, typically using the learned dynamics as differentiable simulator to generate trajectories for policy optimization. An early example is Ramesh and Ravindran (2023), which compared dynamics learning with black-box MLP and DeLaN. They evaluated the method on pendulum, cartpole, and acrobot systems, where DeLaN achieve better performance and sample efficiency. Kotecha et al. (2025) evaluated multiple inertial parameterizations using DeLaN for locomotion. The learned dynamics were used within MPC and evaluated on simulated quadruped, showing improved prediction accuracy and sample efficiency. Li et al. (2024a) learned DeLaN-based transition model, with Stribeck friction model and kinematic manipulator model. The transition model was used as simulator for RL, where the policy optimizes computed-torque controller gains instead of torques directly, with validation on real manipulator.

Giacomuzzo et al. (2024) extended further Lagrangianinspired polynomial kernel to learn the kinetic and potential energies of manipulator, achieving data-efficient inversedynamics identification. Guo et al. (2024) trained DeLaN for lower-limb exoskeleton dynamics and used GPR to compensate for the remaining residual errors while quantifying uncertainty. The resulting model was combined with nonlinear extended state observer, and it was used within backstepping controller for human-exoskeleton cooperative motion. Cheng et al. (2016) devised structured RKHS to learn the inverse dynamics and perform trajectory tracking with holonomic rigid-body robots. Specifically, they designed hybrid polynomial kernels to embed the Lagrangian structure of the robot dynamics, and proved that their method converges to the true dynamics with few samples. Discussion: In suitable settings, Lagrangian learning methods offer favorable trade-off between physical consistency, data efficiency, and generality. DeLaN enforce positive definiteness of the inertia matrix by construction and expose interpretable quantities, including M(q), V(q), and the system energy, which can be directly reused in computedtorque, energy-shaping, and MPC controllers. However, their explicit energy decomposition (1) is well suited to rigid-body systems but limits applicability to broader system classes. LNNs recover greater generality by learning the Lagrangian directly, at the cost of losing structure. Several works report higher accuracy and sample efficiency than black-box MLPs models on the same systems (Ramesh and Ravindran 2023). However, validation remains concentrated on low-DoF benchmarks, with applications to floating-base and high-DoF robots only beginning to emerge (Schulze et al. 2026; Kotecha et al. 2025).

Consequently, their application has so far been limited to low-dimensional systems such as pendulums, quadrotors, and wheeled robots.

For instance, Duong and Atanasov formulated port-Hamiltonian dynamics on the (2021a) Lie group SE(3) and combined them with passivity-based control for trajectory tracking, demonstrating the method on simulated quadrotor. Duong et al. (2024) extended this work by incorporating general Lie group constraints and an explicit dissipation term to capture friction and air drag, and validated the method on pendulum systems, ground vehicles, and quadrotors. Jin et al. (2025a) used the port-Hamiltonian framework for SysID of an underwater vehicle, by also learning dissipative and input matrix. Beckers et al. (2023) learned switching port-Hamiltonian dynamics with uncertainty quantification, embedding the energy-based structure of hopping robot model and the switching behavior in GPR prior. similar approach has been used to learn distributed port-Hamiltonian models of soft robotic manipulators in Ali et al. (2026). Discussion: Hamiltonian methods share the interpretability and energy-consistency advantages of Lagrangian formulations. Moreover, the port-Hamiltonian extension models dissipation, actuation, and energy exchange explicitly rather than as residual terms, providing principled treatment of non-conservative effects and natural interface to passivitybased and energy-shaping control. However, because the Hamiltonian is defined in terms of the generalized momenta p, which are rarely measured directly, recovering it from velocities requires either the inertia matrix or learned transformation. Learning with an unstructured MLP also loses the explicit decomposition into inertia and potential energy, unless it is enforced by design (Zhong et al. 2020), while energy consistency over long rollouts still requires structure-preserving integration. Finally, as with Lagrangian methods, SE(3) formulations introduce redundant states, require known kinematic constraints, and have so far been validated primarily on low-DoF robotic platforms.

sections.title: 3.3 Model-Structured Learning Architectures
sections.content: We use the term model-structured learning to denote methods that embed physics priors into learning model (i) designing specialized layers (e.g., architectures by: NN layers) or internal architectural connections derived from physical principles, and/or (ii) enforcing physical consistency through architectural constraints. In the context of NNs , these methods are referred to as MSNNs , term recently introduced in Piccinini et al. (2025b,a). We adopt the broader term model-structured learning to encompass analogous approaches beyond NNs , to unify the fragmented taxonomy used in the literature. Their architectures embed physical principles including force superposition, the quadratic dependence of aerodynamic drag on vehicle speed, and the effect of past control inputs on the current longitudinal acceleration. Da Lio et al. (2020b) proposed MSNNs to learn and control the lateral vehicle dynamics. Their architecture embeds steering characteristics derived from single-track vehicle models (Abe 2009). After learning the forward dynamics, they trained an inverse-model steering controller end-to-end, by backpropagating control losses through the learned dynamics, without additional training data. Subsequent work (Piccinini et al. 2023, 2025a, 2026) extended this approach to driving at the handling limits by embedding local learnable approximations of doubletrack vehicle models. Pagot et al. (2023) introduced MSNN for steering control in automated parking, with neural polynomial layer to learn the nonlinear steering characteristics, and FIR layer to learn the transient dynamics. Da Lio et al. (2023) proposed an MSNN for lateral velocity estimation. They extended the equations of kinematic observer with interpretable neural terms, to estimate the lateral velocity from the measured accelerations, yaw rate, and longitudinal speed. Mungiello et al. (2026) introduced unified autoregressive MSNN to model the coupled longitudinal-lateral vehicle dynamics near the limits. Their architecture uses specialized layers to capture steadystate and transient effects, as well as their coupling. Beyond vehicle dynamics, Antonucci et al. (2021) designed an MSNN for real-time human motion prediction in robotics, by neuralizing social force model and estimating the interaction forces from past pose sequences. Lahoud et al. (2024) introduced MSNN to complement Prepared using sagej.cls 12 Journal Title XX(X) DeLaN and learn friction and inertial effects of robotic manipulator. They designed linear layers to learn the viscous forces and motor inertia (reflecting the linearity of these effects in the joint velocities and accelerations), and two tailored layers to learn the non-symmetrical Coulomb friction forces considering the joint rotation direction. Similarly, Hu et al. (2025) introduced structured layer to learn the joint friction components (viscous, Coulomb, and nonlinear Stribeck effects) within DeLaN architecture for manipulator dynamics learning. Candeo et al. (2026) developed recurrent MSNN for brake pad emission prediction, embedding physical dependencies on brake temperature, vehicle deceleration, and velocity. Pfrommer et al. (2020) devised polytopic NN architecture to learn discontinuous contact dynamics for manipulation systems with frictional impacts and stiction. They parameterized inter-body signed distance functions and contact-frame Jacobians, thus embedding rigid contact mechanics and geometric priors into the model architecture. Deng et al. (2024) proposed an Equation-Embedded NN for inverse dynamics learning in robotic manipulators. The NewtonEuler equations of motion are encoded directly in the NN architecture as specialized layers with compositionoperator activations, while liquid mechanism dynamically adapts inter-layer connections to the input data. Their model achieved competitive torque prediction and parameter identification with limited data, outperforming black-box baselines under varying friction conditions. MSNNs with Physical Constraints: In Chrosniak et al. (2024); Kolluri et al. (2025); Fang and Yu (2025), NNs learned the parameters of single-track vehicle model, while sigmoid activations embedded in the NN architecture constrained the parameters to physically meaningful ranges. Similarly, Yang et al. (2023b) used RNNs with RK4 integration layers to learn the inertial, stiffness and damping parameters of manipulators joints, while enforcing nonnegativity constraints on certain parameters through custom RNN cells. Kamp et al. (2023) introduced neural layers to model mechanical springs and dampers, augmenting vehicles suspension dynamics model with learnable components. They also enforced physical consistency through loss function regularization, e.g., by penalizing non-zero damper forces at zero velocity. In the field of linear motor control, Bolderman et al. (2021) designed structured neural layer to encode the linear effect of friction components, the positivity of the rotor mass, and physics-based weights initialization. Sutanto et al. (2020) learned the inverse dynamics of robot arm with tailored model parametrizations to enforce physical consistency of the learned parameters. Specifically, their training process constrains the positive definiteness of mass and inertia matrices, and the triangular inequality of the principal moments of inertia. For multi-body robotic systems, Djeumou et al. (2022) modeled the dynamics as the sum of known physics-based and learnable neural terms, while enforcing symmetries and contact force relations through architectural constraints on the learnable parts. Model-Structured Learning with Gaussian Processes: Model-structured learning models have also been developed with GPR frameworks. In particular, Beckers et al. (2026) Prepared using sagej.cls incorporated the geometric structure of nonholonomic dynamics into matrix-valued kernel of GPR model, enabling dynamics learning of nonholonomic systems while rigorously certifying constraint satisfaction. Their method was validated on nonholonomic rolling disc, with applications to wheeled robots. Dai et al. (2024) modeled nonlinear friction with dissipative GPR, whose matrix-vector structure enforces passivity and positive semidefiniteness of the damping matrix. Their model was used for aerodynamic friction estimation of an aerial robot. Rezaei-Shoshtari et al. (2019) controlled robot arm using cascaded GPR model arranged along the kinematic chain, inspired by recursive Newton-Euler algorithms, and predicting joint torques recursively from the end-effector to the base or vice versa. Discussion: In many of the previously cited works, MSNNs were compared against general-purpose NNs and learning models (e.g., MLPs and RNNs), demonstrating improved sample efficiency, generalization from limited training data, and better interpretability due to the explicit embedding of physical principles (Da Lio et al. 2020a; Djeumou et al. 2022; Piccinini et al. 2023; Da Lio et al. 2023; Piccinini et al. 2025b; Mungiello et al. 2026). However, the design of model-structured architectures often requires significant engineering effort and domain expertise, and their performance is strongly influenced by the choice of the embedded physical principles and the structure of the architectural layers, connection, and constraints. In Sec. 6.1, we review open-source libraries that facilitate the design of model-structured learning architectures.

NODEs also provide the theoretical foundation for flow matching (Lipman et al. 2023), state-of-the-art approach for imitation learning. Variational Integrator Networks: While NODEs successfully integrate deep learning into continuous-time modeling, they rely on general-purpose numerical integrators (e.g., Runge-Kutta methods) that do not preserve the geometric and energy properties of physical systems. In contrast, Variational Integrators (VIs) (Marsden et al. 2001) leverage discrete variational principles to construct symplectic integrators, naturally preserving the symplectic structure and, under appropriate discrete symmetries, momentum and favorable long-term energy conservation. By leveraging VIs , Saemundsson et al. (2020) proposed Variational Integrator Networks ( VINs) that explicitly match discrete-time equations of motion. Their approach encodes symplecticity, energy and momentum conservation laws as hard architectural constraints, promoting accurate long-term prediction, interpretability, and data-efficient learning. VINs were validated on mechanical systems like pendulums and massspring systems, learning from both noisy observations and directly from image pixels.

sections.title: 3.5 Hybrid Physics-Learning Architectures
sections.content: This body of research combines physics-based models with ML in modular way, where learning-based methods learn specific components of the dynamics or correct the output of physics-based models. Unlike MSNNs , these techniques use learning-based methods as separate modules that interact with physics-based models. This modularity allows for flexible design of the ML components, while still leveraging unchanged physics-based models to capture parts of the system dynamics.

In these works, the NN architectures were general-purpose MLPs , ANFISs (Acosta et al. 2019), and neural-ExpTanh networks (Djeumou et al. 2023a). In Yang et al. The drift term of their SDE combines physics-based rigid-body dynamics with learned neural components for the complex thrust and aerodynamic effects, while the diffusion term provides distance-aware uncertainty estimates outside the training distribution. Taken together, these works demonstrate that NNs can effectively learn complex subsystems of physics-based models, enabling accurate modeling, control and estimation of robotic systems with limited data and domain knowledge.

3.6.2 Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamical
Systems (SINDy): Brunton et al. (2016) introduced SINDy
to discover governing equations from data by selecting
sparse terms from a library of candidate nonlinear functions.
Starting from this seminal work, some authors proposed
methodological extensions of SINDy to embed physics
priors into the learning process. In particular, Chu and
Hayashibe (2020) proposed Lagrangian-SINDy to discover
compact expressions of the total energy and Lagrangian of
multi-DoF systems, using prior knowledge from simpler
subsystems. Lathourakis and Cicirello (2024) proposed
physics-encoded SINDy, which injects known friction
laws and domain biases to capture discontinuous stick-
slip dynamics. Chen et al. (2021b) combined PINNs with
sparse regression to learn governing equations from scarce
and noisy data by embedding residual equations in the
loss. Zolman et al. (2025) combined SINDy with RL to
learn sparse, interpretable models of dynamics, reward, and
policy. Purnomo and Hayashibe (2023) proposed xL-SINDy
to identify sparse Lagrangian expressions via the Euler-
Lagrange equations and a proximal gradient method, with
the option to leverage prior Lagrangian knowledge from
simpler subsystems.
sections.content: Other works applied SINDy variants to learn or control the dynamics of robotic systems, by embedding physics insights into the design of the candidate library and the learning process. Weihmayr et al. (2025) used SINDy to learn the dynamics of vehicle, and integrated the model into an MPC controller for path tracking, showing In Papageorgiou et al. improved results in comparison with physics-based singletrack model. Paparazzo et al. (2025) employed SINDy for online learning of vehicles lateral tire forces, using odd polynomial functions to reflect the symmetry of the lateral forces with respect to the slip angle. They constrained the learnable parameters to be physically meaningful, and into an MPC controller integrated the learned model for (2024), trajectory tracking. SINDy was adopted to learn the dynamics of soft robot, using candidate functions derived from kinematic and dynamic principles, including trigonometric terms to capture rotational dynamics. Liu et al. (2024a) applied SINDy to learn the dynamics of an UMV, using library of physics-inspired candidate functions, derived from Newtons the laws and hydrodynamics. In Buriani et al. (2026), dynamics of jumping quadruped was learned using SINDy in reduced-order, physically-interpretable latent space. Omar et al. (2024) used SINDy to learn the dynamics including friction and payload of robot manipulator, effects. Their candidate functions were designed from EulerLagrange principles, integrating prior knowledge of the robot kinematics and dynamics. They incorporated inequality constraints into SINDy to handle the ill-conditioning that arises from simple excitation trajectories. Chen et al. (2021a) proposed sparse-regression framework for manipulator dynamics learning, where prior knowledge from simpler pendulum systems was used to construct the candidate library for 3-DoF manipulator. They validated the identified model in simulated obstacle-avoidance trajectory planning for manipulator. Bhattacharya et al. (2022) used SINDy with control to discover an interpretable predictive model of robotic soft esophagus directly from pressure Prepared using sagej.cls 16 Journal Title XX(X) and time-of-flight sensor data, without relying on firstprinciples soft-body model. Their model was integrated in an MPC to control robotic esophagus. Bhattacharya et al. (2020) combined reduced-order modeling with SINDy to discover the differential equations of an esophageal swallowing robot from pressure-driven deformation data. Their method was validated on soft robotic esophagus, using measurements from quarter-scale platform and validation on the full system. Shen et al. (2022) cast industrial robot dynamics identification as sparse Bayesian regression problem, using dictionary of candidate robot dynamics terms and recursive online updates to track timevarying behavior. They validated the method on simulated and real SCARA robots. Discussion: Collectively, SINDy-based methods enable the discovery of compact, interpretable robot dynamics by embedding physics priors into the candidate function library and sparse regression process. However, their effectiveness heavily depends on the candidate library and on the coordinates in which the dynamics are expressed: designing both still requires substantial human expertise. Most formulations also regress on state derivatives estimated from noisy measurements, and become ill-conditioned when the excitation trajectories are not sufficiently informative. Finally, phenomena such as contact, hysteresis, and backlash are difficult to capture with compact libraries of candidate functions, so scaling SINDy to high-dimensional, interacting, and contact-rich robotic systems remains an open research challenge.

sections.title: 3.7 Physics-Encoded Neural Operators
sections.content: Neural operators ( NOs ) extend NNs from learning fixeddimensional input-output mappings to learning operators between infinite-dimensional function spaces (Li et al. 2024b; Faroughi et al. 2024). Physics priors can be incorporated into these architectures by embedding governing equations or physical principles into the operator structure (physics-encoded NOs). Table 5 summarizes the papers discussed in this section, and in the sections on physics-informed and physics-guided NOs , indicating the type of operator, the way physics is embedded, and the robot class. Most works in this category focused on Koopman operators for learning the dynamics of robotic systems. Koopman operator theory represents nonlinear dynamics via linear, typically infinite-dimensional operator acting on observable functions of the state (Koopman 1931). In practice, the system is lifted to higher-dimensional space  (Fig. 5)  where its evolution is approximately linear, making Koopman models attractive for learning and control of nonlinear robotic systems. In this setting, the dictionary is the set of lifting functions mapping the state to the lifted space. Its choice critically affects accuracy, interpretability, and control performance. Some works encoded physics through lifted architecture/dictionary design  (Fig. 5)  and consistency constraints. Shi and Karydis (2022) exploited the topological structure of the robots configuration space (for rigid robots) and workspace (for soft robots) to analytically construct polynomial-based Koopman lifting functions via Kronecker products. Their approach was applied for Prepared using sagej.cls dynamics learning with wheeled robot, two-link robotic arm, and soft robotic leg. Similarly, Joglekar et al. (2023) designed Koopman candidate functions for Ackermannsteered vehicles from Lie-bracket constructions informed by holonomic/nonholonomic constraints, and used the learned model for trajectory tracking. To learn the dynamics and control cart-pendulum and spherical mobile robots, Abraham et al. (2017) chose polynomial and Fourier lifting functions inspired by the systems properties, such as pendulum angle periodicity on rotational manifolds. For nonholonomic (2025c) used mobile-robot navigation, Zhang et al. bilinear KoopmanMPC formulation with observables built from physically meaningful kinematic coordinates, including yaw-angle trigonometric embeddings (e.g., cos(), sin()), so the lifted model preserves heading geometry and controlaffine structure under uncertainty. In soft robotics, Shi et al. (2022) analytically designed Koopman lifting functions based on the workspace geometry and pneumatic-actuator structure of soft multi-finger gripper, enabling physicsbased dictionary design for online dynamics learning and control. Castano et al. (2020) exploited the dynamics structure and tail-actuation kinematics of rigid-body robotic fish to construct Koopman lifting functions, with physics-encoded basis-function design for learning and predictive control of soft robotic swimmer dynamics. Wang et al. (2024b) further enforced physical consistency with an energy-preserving Koopman formulation that imposes hard energy-difference matching constraints for Lagrangian systems to improve dynamics learning and trajectory tracking with cart-pole system. The reader can refer to Shi et al. (2026) for other examples of Koopman operators in robot learning. Beyond Koopman methods, Wang et al. (2025b) used KAN for static friction identification in industrial manipulators, retaining physically meaningful values of the trained parameters. Discussion: By lifting nonlinear robot dynamics to an approximately linear latent space, physics-encoded NOs enable linear and bilinear control methods, such as KoopmanMPC, to be applied to nonlinear systems. Constructing the lifting functions from configurationspace topology, kinematic constraints, or actuator structure replaces generic dictionary learning with interpretable observables, and enables physical consistency to be enforced in the lifted space (Shi and Karydis 2022; Abraham et al. 2017; Shi et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2024b). This is particularly valuable for soft and continuum robots, where minimalcoordinate models are difficult to derive. However, designing the lifting functions remains highly application-specific, and no transferable methodology has yet emerged. Moreover, the lifted dimension grows rapidly with the state dimension, limiting current applications to low-DoF systems. Finally, physics-encoded operators beyond the Koopman framework remain largely unexplored.

sections.title:
3.8.2 Bio-inspired Architectures: A complementary line
of research embeds priors derived from biological principles
of perception, action selection, and neural representation
into learning architectures. These methods encode physical
insights in the form of structured computational mechanisms
inspired by natural intelligence.
sections.content: A first class of approaches adopts bio-inspired control architectures, where perception and action are coupled through structured competition mechanisms. For example, layered architectures based on the affordance competition hypothesis (Cisek 2007) were used by Da Lio et al. (2023) for evaluation and selection of multiple candidate actions via dynamical competition process. The resulting architecture embeds action selection as an intrinsic computational mechanism, rather than an explicit optimization step, and was applied to autonomous driving and human-vehicle interaction (Da Lio et al. 2021). second line of work embeds bio-inspired priors into the internal representations of learning models. Inspired by the circular neural structures underlying head-direction encoding in animals, Plebe and Da Lio (2023) proposed circular latent spaces, where rotations are represented as cyclic shifts, establishing direct correspondence between transformations and physical rotations. Similarly, latent Plebe et al. (2021) encoded the cortical magnification principle into occupancy-grid representations through nonuniform spatial warping that allocates higher resolution to nearby regions. Together, these approaches demonstrate how biologically inspired latent spaces and representations can embed domain knowledge directly into the architecture, improving generalization and perception accuracy. Finally, cognitive principles can also guide the learning of latent representations. Inspired by predictive coding and the free-energy principle (Friston 2010), Plebe and Da Lio (2020) structured variational autoencoder around latent variables and future-state prediction. task-relevant By explicitly organizing the latent space according to semantically meaningful concepts (e.g., obstacles and lanes) and predictive objectives, the architecture embeds cognitive priors that improve representation learning, interpretability, and scene prediction. Overall, bio-inspired architectures embed inductive biases through structured control mechanisms, latent representations, and predictive objectives. They capture principles of natural intelligence to promote adaptive behavior and structured representations. Combining them with physicsbased priors and model-structured architectures offers promising direction toward robot learning systems that are both physically grounded and biologically inspired. 3.8.3 Symmetry-Aware Architectures: Besides their role
as geometric priors in data-driven methods, symmetries are
fundamentally linked to conservation laws through Noether’s
theorem (Watson et al. 2025), motivating their use as
inductive biases in robotics. Ordo˜nez-Apraez et al. (2023,
2025) developed a framework to exploit morphological
symmetries as physics-encoded geometric priors in robotics.
They showed how these symmetries can be incorporated
into learning-based methods for dynamics modeling, control,
estimation, and design, either through model architectures
or data augmentation. They showed improved sample
efficiency and generalization over black-box baselines in
centroidal momentum estimation and contact detection
for legged robots. In the same experimental setting, Xie
et al. (2025) proposed a Graph Neural Network (GNN)
that encodes the robot kinematic tree and morphological
symmetries for quadruped dynamics learning, obtaining
improved generalization and data efficiency over black-box
approaches. Su et al. (2024) incorporated morphological
symmetries into RL for legged locomotion and loco-
manipulation tasks, using data augmentation and symmetry-
constrained policy architectures. They achieved improved
sample efficiency and task performance over unconstrained
baselines. Similarly, Li et al. (2025b) used equivariant
policies to enable ambidextrous bimanual manipulation,
demonstrating task transferability across arms in both
simulation and real-robot experiments. Sharma and Fink
(2026) designed a physics-inspired GNN for multi-body
dynamical systems that enforces pairwise conservation of
linear and angular momentum through edge-local reference
frames equivariant to SE(3) symmetries. Their architecture
embeds momentum conservation as a hard inductive bias
in the message-passing design, enabling interpretable and
stable long-horizon predictions. Their method was validated
on 3D granular systems with inelastic collisions, and
was presented in the context of robotics and engineered
mechanical systems.

The combination of data-driven and physicsinformed loss terms can improve generalization in datascarce regions, and hence improve the physical consistency of the learned model. Following the seminal work of Raissi et al. sections.title: 4.1 Physics-Informed Neural Networks
sections.content: Originally proposed for solving complex PDEs across diverse physical domains (Raissi et al. 2019; Meng et al. 2025), PINNs have recently been employed in robotics problems governed by ODEs , where physicsinformed losses complement data-driven objectives to improve generalization in data-scarce regions (Bianchi et al. 2024). We emphasize that, unlike physics-encoded learning, physics-informed learning does not embed physics priors into model architectures, which typically remain conventional feedforward NNs . Instead, physical knowledge is incorporated exclusively through the training loss. Conversely, the physics loss Jphysics penalizes violations of the governing PDE at Nf collocation points. By embedding prior physical knowledge into the training objective, PINNs act as universal function approximators guided to satisfy conservation laws and other physical constraints. In robotics, they have been applied to learn NN surrogates for PDEs arising in soft robotics and continuum mechanics, replacing expensive numerical solvers with real-time models. They have also been used to learn rigid-body dynamics governed by ODEs , where the physics-informed loss improves generalization in data-scarce regions by constraining the NN to satisfy the governing equations. This reduces overfitting and is particularly valuable in robotics, where acquiring large labeled datasets is often expensive or impractical. Table 8 summarizes the works reviewed in this section by application class, including the robot type and the physical principles embedded in their loss functions. Dynamics Learning and Estimation: In vehicle dynamics, Sun et al. (2024) trained an MLP with hybrid loss combining data fitting and physics-based regularization, penalizing deviations from an analytical single-track model. Similarly, Cortese and Lenzo (2026b,a) regularized the training loss of MLPs and LSTMs with multi-body vehicle models to estimate the lateral velocity, outperforming purely data-driven approaches. Additional vehicle applications of PINNs include predicting the energy consumption of electric vehicles (Lim et al. 2024) and learning tractortrailer dynamics (Zeipel et al. 2024). In soft and continuum robotics, Beaber et al. (2024) proposed PINN surrogate framework to predict the deformation of pneumatic soft robots. They embedded the governing continuum-mechanics PDEs as PINN loss, alongside boundary and initial conditions. Once trained, the surrogate replaces expensive PDEs numerical solvers, enabling real-time deformation prediction of soft fingers. Bensch et al. (2024) used PINN to learn the static shape of tendon-driven continuum robot. They integrated the corresponding PDEs into the training loss, with boundary values obtained from shooting-method reference solver. The learned model predicts the full robot shape significantly faster than the reference, enabling use inside sampling-based path planners. Wang et al. (2024c) extended this line in soft grasping by injecting minimum-potential-energy principles from elastic mechanics into the loss of PINN surrogate for Fin-Ray soft robotic fingers. They reported improved deformation prediction over finite-element references after sim-to-real data assimilation. In aerial robotics, Bianchi et al. (2024) applied PINNs to estimate the thrust and drag parameters of quadrotor, embedding the rigid-body equations of motion as ODE residuals in the training loss. With limited flight data, their PINN-based estimator outperforms an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) baseline. Some authors also showed how physics-regularized losses improve robustness under distribution shifts. For example, Serrano et al. (2024) added discretized first-principles consistency term (with slack variables) to sequence predictor for multirotor slung-load systems, and outperformed both pure physical model and data-only baseline. Wang et al. (2025a) combined temporal convolutions with wind-aware physics Prepared using sagej.cls loss for quadrotor dynamics learning, improving prediction and MPC tracking in unknown environments. Liu et al. (2025b) used an online continual physics-informed objective for quadrotor state estimation under wind disturbances, showing improved adaptation during streaming updates. For ground robots, Sahoo and Klein (2026) embedded inertialnavigation constraints into lightweight PINN, and reported drift reduction for pure-inertial mobile robot localization. Control: Bolderman et al. (2022) and Bolderman et al. (2024) combined physics-based model with an MLP to control the dynamics of linear motor. Their loss function contains regularization term that trusts more the physicsbased model in regions of the state space with limited or no training data, thereby improving the models extrapolation capabilities. Bolderman et al. (2024) also derived the conditions for the input-to-state stability of the resulting controller. Nicodemus et al. (2022) employed PINNs for nonlinear MPC with multi-link robotic manipulator. They incorporated control inputs and initial conditions into their NN, allowing PINNs to serve as surrogate models for dynamical systems. Saviolo et al. (2022) presented physicsinformed temporal convolutional network for quadrotor dynamics learning and MPC-based trajectory tracking. They used physics constraints based on Newton-Euler equations as additional loss terms during training, fostering generalization beyond the training distribution. Antonelo et al. (2024) extended standard PINNs to accommodate control inputs and variable-length time horizons via autoregressive chaining. They included the ODE residuals of systems dynamics in the training loss without requiring labeled data. They performed dynamics learning and MPCbased control of nonlinear systems, including Van der Pol oscillator and an electric submersible pump. Li and Xiao (2025) proposed PINN-based input-shaping method to suppress vibrations in flexible single-link robotic arms. Their training loss combines the PDE constraints of flexible beams modal equations with vibration modal conditions, and two-phase training procedure identifies the optimal impulse sequence. Sanyal and Roy (2023) further combined physics and data losses in robust adaptive MPC for quadrotors: an ODE-based physics term regularizes the model under parametric uncertainty, while data term captures residual disturbances, improving trajectory-tracking performance over data-driven MPC baselines. Trajectory Planning: Besides the architectural symmetry discussed in Sec. 3.8, the neural time fields of Ni and Qureshi (2023a, 2024) for time-optimal manipulator motion planning are trained with physics-informed loss built on the residuals of the Eikonal equation (a first-order nonlinear PDE ), which removes the need for expert demonstrations. Lee (2023) modeled contactless handovers between collaborative robots using an LSTM - MLP architecture. Their training relies on physics-informed loss based on energy functions derived from the system dynamics, enabling prediction of the catching points of flying packages. In the context of generative models  (Table 6)  , Gao et al. (2026) trained VLA with adaptive driving styles for vehicle trajectory planning, and used loss term that penalizes violations of kinematic laws on predicted trajectories, improving generalization. 22 Journal Title XX(X) Physics-Informed Losses for Lagrangian & Hamiltonian NNs: DeLaN, LNNs, and HNNs are commonly trained using forward or inverse dynamics errors. Discussion: The main appeal of physics-informed losses is their architectural flexibility: since physics enters only through the training objective, they can be combined with diverse learning models, to LSTMs and VLAs , without modifying their architecture. They also have the potential to reduce reliance on labeled data by training directly from physics-based equation residuals, improve extrapolation in data-scarce regimes, and provide computationally efficient surrogate models for soft and continuum robots (Bensch et al. 2024). from MLPs Their main limitation is the counterpart of this flexibility: physical laws are enforced only as soft training constraints, so low loss residuals do not guarantee exact physical consistency at inference  (Fig. 3)  . sections.title: 4.2 Physics-Informed Neural Operators
sections.content: Physics-informed losses were used to guide neural operator learning when data alone were insufficient. In autonomous driving, Zhang et al. (2026) introduced an acceleration-based physics loss (between predicted and measured accelerations) and combined it with online sliding-window updates, using the method for vehicle dynamics learning with Koopman operator. In soft robotics, Ristich et al. (2025) decomposed the PDE -based dynamics of soft arm into passive physical term and unknown actuation forces. They learned two Koopman operators: one for the physical term, trained with PDE-residual loss from phase-space samples (no trajectory data), and one for the unknown term, learned from trajectories. The two are then combined via Strang splitting. Kamath et al. (2026) trained Koopman neural operator by combining physics-informed loss that penalizes deviations from nominal quadrotor dynamics, and real-data loss from onboard flight experiments. Their model was then embedded in an MPC for trajectory tracking. Tan et al. (2025) proposed physics-informed DeepONet (Lu et al. 2021a) for vehicle dynamics modeling. Their architecture was trained using physics-informed loss built from known linear relations among vehicle states and analytical vehicle models. Sivakumar and Feroskhan (2026) adopted FNO for quadrotor crash-area estimation under actuator failures and wind disturbances. They used custom physics-informed loss function encoding mass conservation. Chen et al. (2024) adopted GNO for autonomous vehicle navigation in traffic networks, and used physics-informed loss to enforce consistency with the Fokker-Planck equation, capturing the dynamics evolution of the vehicles on the graph. Lim et al. (2026) used PINO module to estimate the physical parameters of vehicle (including drag, mass, rolling resistance) from measured speed and acceleration windows, and used hybrid data-plus-physics residual loss.

sections.title: Learning Algorithms
sections.content: This class of methods uses physics-based models to compute structured input features for downstream ML algorithms. To estimate vehicles sideslip angle, Graber et al. (2018) used physics-based kinematic model to provide structured inputs to GRU network, which captures temporal dependencies and compensates for modeling inaccuracies. Similarly, De Groote et al. (2021) used physicsbased model of slider-crank mechanism to compute structured kinematic features for an MLP, improving sample efficiency and generalization while constraining learning to physically consistent representation. Cortese and Lenzo (2026b) used physics-based vehicle model within UKF to generate preliminary estimate of vehicles lateral velocity, which was refined by an MLP. The resulting hybrid estimator outperformed both the standalone UKF and an LSTM. In the context of linear motor control, Bolderman et al. (2021) used physics-guided input layer to encode the dependency of mechanical friction on position and signed velocity, and fed the resulting features to an MLP controller. Hong et al. (2023) adopted an RNN to process the residuals of physics-based model, and used it for quadrotor dynamics learning in an MPC trajectory tracking application. Input features include physically meaningful state variables (e.g., positions, velocities, and control inputs), ensuring that the learned model operates in space aligned with the governing equations of the system. Yang and Zhang (2026) developed driving VWM , and injected physics through dedicated modules in the conditioning pathway: coordinatesystem aligner (relative/absolute motion consistency), an instance-flow guidance module (temporal consistency from 3D flow), and box-coordinate guidance (spatial/occlusion consistency). This supports prediction tasks, and improves downstream estimation and perception metrics.

sections.title: 5.2 Physics-Guided Features & Training Data
sections.content: This category of approaches exploits physics priors to design input features or training data for downstream learning tasks. Lahoud et al. (2024) used DeLaN to learn nonsymmetric Coulomb friction in robot manipulators. Physics priors are embedded through physically meaningful inputs (joint positions, velocities, and accelerations), reflecting the underlying mechanics and friction forces. Also, they designed informative training trajectories, based on finite Fourier series matched to the robots natural modes. Robinson et al. (2022) injected partial knowledge into the hidden layers of the system dynamics of MLPs via engineered input features computed from analytical equations. Applied to mechanical oscillators, this improved training speed and accuracy. Elazab et al. (2026) proposed physics-guided framework for fault detection in quadruped robots. Biomechanics knowledge was embedded through physics-based features derived from raw sensor measurements, including gait symmetry, center of pressure, and an energy proxy. Their two-stage soft-voting architecture outperformed black-box deep learning in simulated fault scenarios. Saleh et al. Other authors incorporated physics primarily through data generation and augmentation. Jin et al. Taken together, these methods provide one of the least invasive ways to embed physics: by acting on features and data, they are compatible with most learning algorithms. Data-centric approaches are particularly attractive, as they address robot data scarcity directly through physics-guided data generation and curation (Jin et al. 2025b; Xu et al. 2025). Their main limitation is that their physics priors do not constrain the learned model or its predictions, and datalevel priors are inactive at inference time. Moreover, feature engineering and excitation design remain largely manual and application-specific, while synthetic data are limited by the fidelity of the underlying simulators.

sections.title: 5.3 Geometric Learning
sections.content: Some approaches modified input and output features to preserve non-Euclidean geometric structures of the data. In the context of IL (Wang et al. 2022) and RL (Alhousani et al. 2023) with collaborative robot manipulators, input data were projected onto the tangent space of target manifold (e.g., SO(3) or symmetric and positive definite matrices), training was performed there, and outputs were mapped back to the manifold. James and Abbeel (2022) developed RL neural policy parametrization that leverages the Bingham distribution to model uncertainty over 3D rotations, allowing policy search to directly sample points in SO(3) for robotic manipulation. Chen and Lipman (2023) introduced Riemannian flow matching framework for navigation, where the input is preprocessed to define geometrically-consistent target vector field, and Riemannian integration step is used to produce the output. Their loss function is formally equivalent to standard flow matching, although it uses geometrically-consistent vector field as target. Riemannian flow matching was also used by Chisari et al. (2024) to learn robotic manipulation policies from point cloud observations. the exploitation of geometric priors in input representations was shown to improve learning performance in tasks involving rotations and geometric constraints, by preserving the underlying manifold structure of the data. sections.title: 5.4 Frequency-Domain Learning
sections.content: A series of works proposed to transform data into the frequency domain to improve learning performance. We regard these methods as physics-guided only when the retained frequency components, or the structure imposed on Prepared using sagej.cls them, follow from known physical properties of the system. Falco et al. (2019) proposed frequency-domain descriptor of human motion for human-robot interaction, explicitly exploiting the biomechanical property that human motion contains no significant frequency components beyond 10 Hz. This bound sets the cut-off of the representation and yields both compression and invariance to the duration of the action. The same principle was employed by Shah et al. (2016), where the low-pass bandwidth of human actions produces compact descriptor of segmented actions, whose size is independent of the motion duration. Wu et al. (2025) used DCT for the individualized modeling of lower-limb joint kinematics in prosthetics. Here, the transform is applied to gait cycles normalized by the gait phase, so that the periodicity of the representation follows from the cyclic nature of human locomotion, while the number of retained coefficients is selected with cumulative-energy criterion.

sections.title: Representations
sections.content: Some authors designed Video World Models ( VWMs) with explicit measures to enforce physically consistent representations in the generated videos  (Table 6)  . In autonomous driving, the VWM of Yang et al. Their generated videos were shown to improve motion prediction. Zhou et al. (2026) added physical condition generator to transform infeasible trajectories from planners/simulators into physically consistent ones before video generation. This was coupled with physicsenhanced multi-view video generator, trained on mixed real and simulated scenarios, targeting robust planning and prediction in autonomous driving. In manipulation, Mao et al. (2025) coupled VWM -based video generation with physical world reconstruction, and learned an object-centric residual policy in the reconstructed simulator. Li et al. (2025a) trained VWM for non-prehensile manipulation by identifying rigid-body dynamics parameters (inertia, friction, and restitution terms) from visual observations, using differentiable physics simulator and GaussianSplatting rendering loss. The resulting VWM embeds contact-rich physical priors into the learned dynamics, and uses physics-aware randomization to generate digital cousins for robust policy transfer in pushing and poking tasks. Wang et al. This makes their learned VWM physically grounded for contact-rich prediction and planning in manipulation. Yuan et al. (2023) improved the physical consistency of humanoid motions generated by VWM . Their method projects generated motions onto physically plausible trajectories produced by an imitation policy trained in physics simulator. The projection module is embedded directly into the diffusion denoising network. Romero et al. (2025) imposed object-level kinematic masks to guide the training of VWMs and improve kinematic consistency and moving object interactions, with potential applications in scene prediction for manipulation tasks. These methods show that physics-guided world representations can improve the physical plausibility of generated videos, benefiting downstream planning, prediction, and control. However, most rely on external physics models, such as differentiable simulators, imitation policies, or VLMs, with only few differentiating through contact dynamics end-toend (Wang et al. 2026a). Consequently, physical consistency depends on the fidelity of the external models and estimated parameters. Moreover, visual realism remains distinct from physical validity, and the scarcity of standardized dynamicsaware metrics makes physical consistency difficult to assess (Sec. 7). Current approaches also focus mainly on rigid-body dynamics, with deformation and articulated contact receiving limited attention.

sections.title: Generation
sections.content: The papers in this category used physics-based guidance to steer diffusion-based generative models  (Table 6)  . Lv et al. (2026) designed kinematics-aware diffusion policy for whole-body robot arm control. They represented states and actions in 3D node space on the robot arm, and constrained the diffusion process with analytical kinematic mappings between the node space and the robots joint space, thus enforcing kinematic feasibility of the generated actions. Du and Song (2025) augmented the diffusion denoising process for manipulation tasks with guidance gradient from an external dynamics model: predicted outcomes are compared with desired conditions, and their differentiable metric is backpropagated into action denoising, enabling post-hoc behavior steering without retraining the base policy. Tucker et al. (2026) applied similar principle to aerial manipulation: foundation VLA policy is adapted with real-time chunking and payload-aware guidance terms. They injected gradient-based guidance corrections at inference to maintain dynamic feasibility under mass and underactuation changes. Xu et al. (2024) used dynamics guidance in diffusion sampling for manipulator design generation: learned differentiable dynamics model provides gradients that steer denoising toward task-effective interaction profiles. Ma et al. (2024) used low-level kinematics-aware diffusion controller for manipulation. They exploited differentiable kinematics to distill end-effector pose trajectories into joint-space diffusion trajectories, thus enforcing kinematic feasibility for multi-task manipulation. Prepared using sagej.cls Taken together, these methods show that physics guidance is an effective mechanism for steering diffusion models toward physically feasible solutions without modifying their architecture or retraining the base model. By injecting kinematic or dynamic knowledge during sampling, they improve task performance while preserving the flexibility and generative capabilities of diffusion-based policies.

sections.title: 5.7 Physics-Guided Neural Operators
sections.content: Some works embedded physics into Koopman neural operators through guided transformations on inputs and observables. Mamakoukas et al. (2021) augmented observables with estimated time derivatives of the state, so the lifted representation explicitly includes kinematic and dynamic rates, rather than only positions. They validated the method for dynamics learning and control of an inverted pendulum and tail-actuated robotic fish. In differential-drive robot setting, Rosenfelder et al. (2025) incorporated first-principles nonholonomic geometry and dynamics by parametrizing the states and inputs assuming rolling-without-slipping, in both kinematic and second-order forms. They showed that purely data-driven Koopman models fail to recover these structures (data does not replace geometry). To learn quadrotor dynamics, Zinage and Bakolas (2022) and Narayanan et al. (2023) adopted SE(3)-consistent states (rigid-body pose with velocities) and physics-based observables derived from rotation matrices and nonlinear systems topology, aligning the Koopman representation with flight kinematics and dynamics. Narayanan et al. (2023) further embedded their model in an MPC for trajectory tracking. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2025a) adopted structured high-dimensional state from bicycle/needle kinematics, so their Koopman-based path tracking MPC evolves in variables that directly encode the curvature-constrained motion of flexible robotic needle. Tan et al. (2025) used physics-based kinematic and dynamic vehicle models to preprocess the inputs of DeepONet for vehicle dynamics learning, and showed improved performance over an LSTM and physical models. Physics-guided NOs provide the least intrusive route to operator learning, redefining only the states and observables while leaving the architecture and training loss unchanged. This also alleviates the dictionary-design challenge of physics-encoded operators (Sec. 3.7). Rosenfelder et al. (2025) showed that physics-guided structures must be supplied rather than learned, as purely data-driven Koopman models failed to recover the nonholonomic geometry of differential-drive robot. However, these methods require known kinematic models, and rely on manually designed, platform-specific observables. By acting only on the inputs, they do not constrain the learned operator and cannot guarantee physically consistent predictions.

These frameworks, however, primarily target differential-equation solving rather than robotics, leaving embedded deployment and closed-loop integration to users. For the physics-guided route (Sec. 5), differentiable simulators are among the primary enabling tools, supporting physically consistent data generation and gradient-based optimization through simulation. Nimble provides differentiable rigid-body contacts, Brax and Warp emphasize massively parallel GPU simulation, TDS offers lightweight targets control-oriented C++/CUDA engine, and Dojo.jl workflows. Conversely, inference-time physics guidance (Sec. 5.6) remains largely unsupported by dedicated software and is typically implemented within task-specific diffusion pipelines.

sections.title: 6.7 Discussion
sections.content: Overall, the reviewed software ecosystem comprises complementary frameworks that support different aspects of physics-embedded machine learning. Consequently, practitioners must combine multiple tools according to the requirements of the robotics application and the chosen physicsembedding paradigm. key limitation is that no existing framework supports physics-guided, physics-encoded, and physics-informed learning within unified workflow spanning model definition, training, evaluation, deployment, and embedded execution. Developing interoperable software abstractions that seamlessly integrate these complementary paradigms, together with differentiable solvers, uncertainty quantification, and standardized benchmarking, remains an open research direction. Such ecosystems would simplify rapid prototyping, reproducible evaluation, and the deployment of physics-embedded learning algorithms on real-world robotic platforms.

sections.title: Challenges
sections.content: Practitioners implementing the methods reviewed in this survey face fragmented software ecosystem, with frameworks typically supporting only specific classes of physics-embedded learning. Despite the rapid progress survey, embedding physics priors in robot learning methods remains an open research field. We organize the main open questions and challenges around the following themes. reviewed in this Prepared using sagej.cls 30 Journal Title XX(X) Challenge 1 Generality versus Physics-based Inductive Bias: fundamental trade-off exists between the flexibility of data-driven learning and the inductive bias introduced by physics priors. The success of foundation models suggests that large-scale pre-training can yield remarkable generalization. However, unlike language and vision, robotics remains fundamentally data-limited due to the cost of real-world experiments, hardware, safety constraints, and the variability of physical interactions. Moreover, it remains unclear whether large-scale pre-training alone can produce models that inherently respect physical laws. Key questions therefore arise: Which physics priors should be embedded, and how strongly should they constrain learning? Incorrect or incomplete priors may introduce structural bias, while overly restrictive priors may limit model expressiveness.

sections.content: the appropriate amount and fidelity of embedded physics are problemdependent. Strong architectural priors, such as energy-based parameterizations in DeLaN and HNNs (Lutter et al. 2019b; Greydanus et al. 2019; Gupta et al. 2020), were found to improve sample efficiency and physically plausible extrapolation when data are scarce. Hybrid approaches that retain an analytical backbone while learning residual dynamics (Bolderman et al. 2024; Schulze et al. 2025; Duong and Atanasov 2021b; Dikici et al. 2025) provide practical compromise between physical structure and flexibility, while partially compensating for modeling errors. More broadly, smooth rigid-body dynamics benefit from stronger structural constraints, whereas contact-rich and highly nonlinear systems require greater flexibility (Pfrommer et al. 2020; Djeumou et al. 2023b). Despite these insights, the field still lacks principled guidelines for selecting appropriate physics priors and determining how strongly they should be embedded for given robotics application. Challenge 2 Reusable and Scalable Physics Priors: related challenge is the design of reusable and scalable physics priors. Most reviewed methods embed knowledge retailored to specific robot, engineering when applied to different embodiments, tasks, or operating conditions. requiring substantial Key questions are: Which physics priors are invariant across robots and tasks? How can reusable physical structure be separated from robot-specific components? Can physicsencoded architectures be composed of transferable building blocks rather than engineered individually for each platform? Several works provide promising directions within restricted settings. Context-conditioned and adaptive formulations (Schulze et al. 2025; Duong and Atanasov 2021b; Djeumou et al. 2023b; Mungiello et al. 2026) improve robustness across operating conditions without retraining from scratch. Modular and equivariant architectures (Lu et al. 2022; Sharma and Fink 2026) promote reusable physical structure, while the MSNNs of Mungiello et al. (2026); Piccinini et al. (2025a); Da Lio et al. (2020b) reuse modular components, such as neural FIRs and local model decompositions, across vehicle dynamics learning tasks. Nevertheless, current methods remain largely confined to closely related robots and shared morphologies. Transferring Prepared using sagej.cls across substantially different embodiments, contact conditions, sensing modalities, and actuation mechanisms still requires considerable redesign. Developing compositional physics priors and reusable architectural building blocks that separate invariant physical structure from robot-specific components therefore remains central challenge. Challenge 3 Physics Priors under Model Mismatch and Sim-to-Real Transfer: Since real-robot data are expensive, physics-embedded models are often developed and trained in simulation (Muratore et al. 2022). central question is therefore how inaccuracies in the assumed physics influence the behavior of physics-embedded models. While embedded priors can improve generalization and sim-to-real transfer, inaccurate assumptions may introduce structural bias that additional data alone cannot eliminate. Key questions are: Which physics priors remain valid across the reality gap? Which components should be adapted online, and which can remain fixed? How can sim-to-real transfer failures be attributed to modeling assumptions? The reviewed literature suggests that embedded structure facilitates transfer when the underlying physics remains the approximately invariant. For example, EulerLagrange formulation transfers directly, requiring only M(q) and V(q) to be learned or fine-tuned on real data. Physics-informed losses have also been shown to improve out-of-distribution generalization (Saviolo et al. 2022), allowing learning to rely on physical priors in datascarce regions (Bolderman et al. 2024). in DeLaN, Conversely, embedded priors can become detrimental when the assumed model omits the dominant sources of error, such as friction, contacts, compliance, or actuator dynamics (Muratore et al. 2022). The resulting mismatch introduces systematic errors that learned residuals can only partially compensate, reducing physical parameter interpretability and weakening theoretical guarantees. At the same time, these failures are often informative, as they reveal which physical assumptions are no longer valid and therefore require refinement. i.e., interpretability, Challenge 4 Interpretability, Explainability, and Trust: One of the main motivations for embedding physics priors is to improve model to which model parameters or functions admit physical interpretation. However, combining analytical models with data-driven learning may weaken this correspondence, causing learned parameters to lose their physical meaning. related challenge is explainability, i.e., understanding why model produced given prediction, which is particularly important in safety-critical robotics applications. the extent Key questions include: Are the learned physical components interpretable using physical principles? Can we identify which embedded prior drives prediction? Can models provide human-understandable explanations? How can trust and effective debugging be supported in real-world deployments? Some reviewed works partially address interpretability. For example, MSNNs explicitly associate learned submodules with physical effects, enabling interpretation of the individual trained parameters (Mungiello et al. 2026; Da Lio et al. 2020b). Challenge 5 Assessing Physical Consistency: Assessing the physical consistency of learned models remains poorly standardized across the literature. Existing works evaluate different notions of consistency depending on the application. Energy-based methods quantify energy conservation, passivity, or power consistency (Greydanus et al. 2019; Lutter et al. 2019b; Lutter and Peters 2021; Lutter et al. 2019a). Equivariant models assess momentum conservation, symmetry preservation, or long-horizon rollout stability (Sharma and Fink 2026). Contact-aware methods measure non-penetration, frictional consistency, or complementarity violations (Pfrommer et al. 2020), while physicsinformed approaches typically evaluate residuals of governing NewtonEuler, ODEs, or PDEs equations (Sanyal and Roy 2023; Sivakumar and Feroskhan 2026). Additional metrics include constraint violations, conservation-law residuals, and trajectory feasibility. Despite their usefulness, these metrics remain fragmented, assessing different aspects of physical consistency over different prediction horizons, perturbation scenarios, and tasks, making direct comparisons difficult. This limitation is particularly evident for VWMs, where visually realistic rollouts may still violate physical laws (Li et al. 2026). Although recent VWMs increasingly report dynamics-aware metrics (Wang et al. 2026b; Li et al. 2025a; Shang et al. 2026), standardized evaluation protocol has yet to emerge. second limitation concerns benchmarks. Current evaluations remain largely tied to paper-specific datasets, simulators, and experimental setups, even when using common differentiable simulation frameworks (Freeman et al. 2021; Macklin et al. 2024; Heiden et al. 2021). Likewise, recent multi-platform datasets (Schulze et al. 2026) improve reproducibility, but no benchmark currently provides unified protocol for evaluating physical consistency across different robotic domains. key research direction is therefore the development of standardized metrics and benchmark suites that assess complementary aspects of physical consistency, including conservation laws, constraint satisfaction, long-horizon prediction, uncertainty calibration, and closed-loop behavior.
